content.title: About
content.content: Bacon is smoked or cured pork belly that is widely used in cooking to add a rich, savory flavor and aroma to dishes. When paired with vegetables, bacon contributes smoky notes, a juicy texture, and enhances the overall taste profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon dates back to ancient Rome, where pork was salted and dried for preservation.
The word “bacon” comes from the Old French “bacon,” meaning “pork.”
In the United States, more than 18 million tons of bacon are consumed each year.
Bacon is a staple in one‑pot meals such as soups, stews, casseroles, and salads.
Cold‑smoked and hot‑smoked methods produce different flavors and textures in bacon.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Bacon provides complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron in bacon helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium has antioxidant properties and supports thyroid health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bacon is often heavily salted, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large amounts of saturated fat may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Nitrates and nitrites
items.content: Curing and smoking can introduce nitrates/nitrites, which in high doses are considered potentially carcinogenic.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crisp the bacon in a pan and add it to vegetable salads, stews, casseroles, or use it as a flavor base for sauces. For a lighter option, slice thinly, quick‑sauté, and toss with sautéed vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bacon refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 6 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration—signs of spoilage include sour smell and grayish color.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef lung is an organ meat from cattle, with a light, spongy, mildly flavored flesh. It is traditionally eaten in several cuisines, including Central Asian, Eastern European, and Middle Eastern dishes, where it is boiled, stewed, or used in sausages and fillings. Its sale for human consumption is restricted or banned in some countries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef lung has a light, spongy texture and a mild flavor.
It is used in traditional dishes in Central Asia, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and elsewhere.
Lung is lower in fat than many other organ meats.
In some countries, such as the United States, the sale of lung for human food is prohibited for food safety reasons.
Lung must be thoroughly cleaned and boiled, and it is usually cooked for a long time.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Beef lung provides protein with relatively little fat.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Beef lung contains iron, which supports oxygen transport.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Unlike most meats, lung contains some vitamin C.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12 and copper
items.content: These nutrients support red blood cell formation and metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Lung is lean compared with many other cuts.

items.title: Legal restrictions and food safety
items.content: Lung can contain fluids and contaminants from the airways and stomach, which is why it is banned in some countries. Buy it only from a source permitted by local regulations.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Lung spoils quickly and must be very fresh and cooked thoroughly, to at least about 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Cholesterol and purines
items.content: Lung contains cholesterol and purines, which matters for people with certain conditions such as gout.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Organs can accumulate environmental contaminants, so eat lung in moderation and choose reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef lung is usually thoroughly rinsed, boiled for a long time until firm, then sliced and fried, stewed, or added to soups, fillings, and sausages. It is often cooked with onions, spices, and herbs to improve its flavor. Where it is legal, buy it only from a reliable, regulated source.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Beef lung is highly perishable. Keep it refrigerated and cook it within a day, or freeze it for longer storage. Cooked lung should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within a day or two. Discard any lung that smells off.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free bread is a baked product made from gluten‑free ingredients such as rice, corn, buckwheat or tapioca flour. It is intended for people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or those who choose a gluten‑free diet. Flavor and texture can differ from traditional wheat bread, but modern formulations achieve a soft crust and airy crumb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first gluten‑free breads appeared in the 1970s in the United States as a response to the rising number of celiac patients.
Gluten‑free blends often contain xanthan gum or guar gum to mimic the elasticity of gluten.
There are more than 30 types of gluten‑free flours, each giving the bread its own distinct taste and color.
Some gluten‑free breads are fortified with probiotics and prebiotics to support gut microbiota.
In Russia, gluten‑free bread became popular in the 2010s and is now available in most major supermarkets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Gluten‑free bread contains no gluten, which can trigger intestinal inflammation in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Bread made from whole‑grain gluten‑free flours (e.g., buckwheat) typically has a lower glycemic index than regular wheat bread.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Many recipes include psyllium, flax seeds or whole grains, boosting dietary fiber content.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortified versions may contain iron, vitamin B12 and folate, nutrients often lacking in a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in gluten‑free bread provide steady energy without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some gluten‑free breads contain high amounts of sugar, salt or fats to improve taste.

items.title: Allergy to other ingredients
items.content: Recipes may include nuts, soy or dairy, which can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Lower protein levels
items.content: Gluten‑free bread often has less protein than wheat bread, so it should be paired with other protein sources.

items.title: Shelf‑life
items.content: Without gluten, the crumb structure can be less stable, causing the bread to stale more quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gluten‑free bread works well for sandwiches, toast, serving alongside soups and salads. It can be toasted, used for breading, or made into croutons. When stored in the refrigerator it stays softer longer than at room temperature.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep gluten‑free bread in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, freeze it, preferably sliced into portions. Before use, allow it to thaw at room temperature or warm it in a toaster.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-grilled-with-sauce.title: Chicken, NS as part, grilled with sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. This version uses boneless chicken breast grilled with a flavorful sauce. The skin is left on and eaten, adding taste and beneficial fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken meat is rich in protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.
Grilling preserves most nutrients while imparting a characteristic smoky aroma.
Chicken can be raised in various systems: free‑range, intensive, and organic.
Chicken skin contains monounsaturated fats and vitamin E.
There are many sauces for chicken: barbecue, teriyaki, honey‑mustard, and more.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low fat (without skin)
items.content: Removing the skin makes chicken a low‑calorie source of energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are involved in metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium, and zinc – important for immune function.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of high protein and moderate fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces are often high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Fat in skin
items.content: Skin increases calorie count and saturated fat, which may be undesirable on low‑fat diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be enjoyed hot or cold, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, incorporated into Asian dishes, or served with vegetable and grain sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions – up to 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: French toast consists of bread slices dipped in a mixture of eggs, milk, and spices, then fried until golden. The “plain” version contains no added toppings such as fruit, syrup, or butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in France in the 17th century and was originally called “pain perdu” – “lost bread”.
It was traditionally used to revive stale bread, turning it into a tasty, nutritious meal.
Dense breads like baguette or thick-sliced sandwich bread work best for the recipe.
In the United States French toast is often served with maple syrup, but the plain version is considered healthier.
There are many variations: with cinnamon, vanilla, or even savory cheese versions.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Milk contributes calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and milk are rich in B2, B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from bread and fats from eggs offers a quick energy boost.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: A plain preparation contains no added sugars, fitting moderate sugar intake guidelines.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or lactose may experience reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Using a lot of butter or oil for frying can make the dish calorie‑rich.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional bread contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve French toast hot; you may sprinkle cinnamon, add fresh berries, nuts, or a drizzle of honey if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days and reheated in a skillet or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Red homemade salsa is a sauce made from ripe tomatoes, fresh onion, garlic, chili peppers, lime juice, and aromatic herbs. It has a bright, slightly spicy flavor and a rich aroma, perfect for Mexican dishes, snacks, and grilled foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally salsa is made without added vinegar, preserving the natural freshness of the vegetables.
The red color comes from ripe tomatoes and sometimes a touch of paprika.
Salsa can be kept in the refrigerator for up to a week, but its flavor is best within the first 2‑3 days.
In Mexico, "salsa fresca" refers to a fresh, uncooked version of the sauce.
Homemade salsa can contain probiotics if fermented ingredients like sauerkraut are added.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes in salsa provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and skin.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Lime and tomatoes deliver a high amount of vitamin C, boosting the immune system.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Salsa is low in calories, making it an excellent addition to weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Onion and tomatoes add fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory compounds
items.content: Garlic and chili contain compounds that help reduce inflammation.

items.title: Spicy food
items.content: The chili content may irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tomatoes or onion.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, monitor the amount, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial contamination; keep refrigerated and use clean utensils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve salsa with nachos, tacos, burritos, grilled meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. It can be used as a marinade, mixed into salads, or enjoyed as a fresh dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store salsa in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach dip, yogurt based is a smooth sauce made from fresh spinach, natural yogurt, garlic, lemon juice and seasonings. It has a creamy texture, light tanginess and a vivid green color, making it perfect for snacks, vegetable sticks and Mediterranean dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yogurt base makes the dip lighter and richer in probiotics compared with mayonnaise‑based versions.
Spinach provides more than 20 vitamins and minerals, including vitamin K, vitamin A and iron.
Greek yogurt, often used in the recipe, has higher protein and lower fat than regular yogurt.
The dip can be prepared at home in 10‑15 minutes using frozen spinach.
Flavor and color remain stable in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt and spinach together supply vitamin B12 and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Probiotics in yogurt promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Carotenoids and lutein from spinach protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Yogurt adds about 5 g of protein per 100 g of dip while keeping calories moderate.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium from yogurt and vitamin K from spinach help strengthen bone tissue.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from the yogurt.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to dairy can trigger reactions to the yogurt base.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: When salt is added, monitor total sodium, especially for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Green leaf oxidation
items.content: Prolonged storage can cause loss of bright color and flavor of the spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip cold with vegetable sticks, crackers, or as a sauce for grilled meat and fish. It can also be spread on sandwiches, added to burritos, or used as a salad dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Shelf life is 5‑7 days. Before use, check for off‑smell or discoloration; discard if any sour or unpleasant odor appears.
